paragraphs: The paper studies how to locate points in a scene that attract several people’s attention at once. When multiple gaze directions meet in three dimensions, that meeting point provides evidence of shared attention. A group can have several such points, so the task involves estimating both their number and their locations from head-mounted video.

The method represents each person’s gaze as a cone-shaped probability distribution extending from the eyes. This accommodates eye movement relative to the head instead of treating the camera’s direction as an exact gaze measurement. The distribution is calibrated using the fixed relationship between the primary gaze direction and the camera pose, then contributes to a shared three-dimensional saliency field.

The algorithm searches for peaks in this field to identify gaze concurrences, using a procedure with a convergence guarantee. The authors reconstruct multiple attention points in real scenes and compare them quantitatively with motion-capture measurements. This connects an uncertain model of individual gaze to a spatial estimate of group attention.
neurips-2012-3d-social-saliency-from-hea.tldr: The method combines uncertain gaze estimates from head-mounted cameras to locate multiple points of shared attention in three dimensions.

paragraphs: The paper introduces MWEM, an algorithm for releasing data under differential privacy. Its central contribution is to bring strong theoretical guarantees together with a procedure the authors describe as straightforward to implement. The practical question is whether a private release method can offer both rigorous assurances and useful accuracy on actual datasets.

MWEM combines two named ingredients: the Exponential Mechanism and the Multiplicative Weights update rule. The contribution is their combination in a data-release algorithm. This gives the paper a clear methodological focus: a relatively simple construction is used to obtain guarantees that the authors report as the best known and close to optimal.

The authors also report experiments in which MWEM is more accurate on real datasets than existing techniques. That is an empirical comparison for the evaluations they conducted. Together, the theoretical and experimental findings support the paper’s practical message: simplicity of implementation can coexist with strong privacy-related guarantees and competitive accuracy in released data.
neurips-2012-a-simple-and-practical-algo.tldr: MWEM combines the Exponential Mechanism with Multiplicative Weights to provide nearly optimal theoretical guarantees and improved empirical accuracy for private data release.

paragraphs: Many sparse learning problems combine a smooth measure of prediction error with a penalty that is not smooth, such as the trace norm. This combination makes optimization challenging. The paper addresses a gap in existing approaches: some apply only when a matrix norm appears as a constraint, while others have weaker convergence rates.

The proposed boosting method handles regularized learning and guarantees accuracy epsilon within O(1/epsilon) iterations. It also alternates boosting steps with local optimization at a fixed rank. These local steps use an objective that is simpler than in previous work, providing an additional way to accelerate training beyond the basic iteration guarantee.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on large-scale problems and demonstrate the method in latent multiview learning. For that application, they supply what they describe as the first efficient weak oracle. The paper therefore links an optimization guarantee, a practical acceleration strategy, and an application-specific computational ingredient needed to make the approach useful.
neurips-2012-accelerated-training-for-ma.tldr: A boosting-based optimizer gives an O(1/epsilon) iteration guarantee for matrix-norm regularization and gains further speed from fixed-rank local optimization.

paragraphs: The paper tackles a hardware bottleneck in reservoir computing: extracting the output quickly enough to benefit from fast internal processing. Time-multiplexed hardware reservoirs had already reached performance comparable to digital implementations, and optoelectronic systems had achieved speeds suitable for real-time operation. Slow digital processing in the readout layer remained an obstacle.

The authors design an analog readout specifically for time-multiplexed optoelectronic reservoir computers. Its purpose is to make the output stage operate in real time as well. This matters because accelerating the reservoir alone does not resolve a delay introduced when its activity is converted into the system’s usable output.

The readout is physically built and evaluated on a standard benchmark task. The authors report performance above non-reservoir methods, while noting room for further improvement. The result is an experimental demonstration that a major readout limitation can be overcome, helping connect fast reservoir hardware with an output mechanism capable of keeping pace.
neurips-2012-analog-readout-for-optical-.tldr: An experimentally tested analog readout enables real-time output from time-multiplexed optoelectronic reservoir computers.

paragraphs: The paper studies when optimizing a substitute training loss remains aligned with the actual costs of multiclass prediction. Those costs are specified by a loss matrix, allowing different mistakes to have different consequences. The authors extend classification calibration to this general setting and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a surrogate loss to satisfy it.

They then define classification calibration dimension: the smallest prediction-space dimension in which a convex, calibrated surrogate can be constructed for a given loss matrix. This turns a design question into a measurable property of the learning problem. The issue is how much representational space a suitable convex surrogate needs.

Upper and lower bounds on this dimension allow the authors to analyze several loss matrices. One application concerns the difficulty of constructing low-dimensional consistent convex surrogates for pairwise subset ranking. The resulting framework supplies a way to investigate both possibilities and obstacles in surrogate design, with broader usefulness presented as a prospect.
neurips-2012-classification-calibration-.tldr: The paper characterizes calibrated multiclass surrogate losses and bounds the prediction-space dimension needed to construct convex ones.

paragraphs: The paper develops an algorithm for dividing a sparse, unweighted graph into groups with relatively dense internal connections and few connections between groups. Here, even connections within a group can be very rare, and their density may shrink as the graph grows. This makes genuine group structure harder to distinguish from noise.

The central insight concerns two kinds of disagreement with a proposed grouping: absent edges inside a group and present edges between groups. A clustering method must balance these errors. The authors argue that sparse graphs require different penalties for the two, making the treatment of missing connections a central design choice.

They analyze the algorithm under the planted partition model, also known as the stochastic block model. In that setting, they show recovery capabilities for sparser graphs and smaller clusters than previous methods. Experiments display the same advantage. The theoretical comparison is tied to this model, while the empirical results support the usefulness of the penalty choice.
neurips-2012-clustering-sparse-graphs-52.tldr: Differently penalizing missing internal edges and existing cross-cluster edges improves clustering of sparse graphs under the planted partition model.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way that neurons could compactly represent a sparse probability distribution over many variables. It applies compressive sensing to the distribution itself, yielding exponential compression. The compressed quantities are expected values of nonlinear functions of the variables, so the representation stores summaries of uncertainty rather than an explicit probability for every possibility.

These expectations can be estimated from samples. The authors state that the quality of the resulting compressed representation is then limited only by sampling quality. They also show that compression preserves the geometric structure of sparse probability distributions, allowing probabilistic computations to take place directly in the compressed representation.

Functions meeting the compressive-sensing requirements can be implemented by simple perceptrons. If perceptrons are treated as models of feedforward neural computation, the mean activity of relatively few neurons could implicitly encode a high-dimensional joint distribution without relying on noise correlations. This is presented as a hypothesis for neural probability coding, rather than an observation establishing that brains use it.
neurips-2012-compressive-neural-represen.tldr: Compressive sensing provides a theoretical mechanism by which a small neural population could encode sparse, high-dimensional probability distributions.

paragraphs: The paper examines how recognition performance depends on an agent’s ability to control what it senses. Its setting is visual search for an object in an otherwise known, static scene. This makes sensing control part of the recognition problem: performance depends on the observations an agent can obtain as well as the information it already has.

The authors propose a measure of control authority and relate it to expected recognition risk. They also connect control to conditional entropy of the posterior distribution, used as a proxy for that risk. The relationship is studied analytically and through simulations using an image-formation model that includes scaling and occlusion.

The analysis describes two extremes within this framework. A passive agent supplied with training data has no performance guarantees beyond those supported by its priors. An agent with unlimited control authority can approach arbitrarily good performance asymptotically. The latter conclusion depends on an idealized control capability and concerns limiting behavior.
neurips-2012-controlled-recognition-boun.tldr: The paper relates visual recognition guarantees to sensing control, from passive observation to asymptotically powerful unlimited control.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to fit mixture models to several related datasets together. A mixture describes complex data through component models, and related datasets may benefit from sharing some of those components. The challenge is to express their statistical connections without forcing every dataset into the same rigid sharing pattern.

The authors introduce latent Dirichlet processes that act as sources of components, called atoms. Each dataset’s mixture combines subsampled versions of these sources. A single mixture can draw atoms from multiple sources, and an individual atom can appear in several mixtures. This creates a many-to-many pattern of sharing across datasets and latent sources.

That flexibility distinguishes the construction from approaches organized around trees or chains. The authors also derive a sampling algorithm that jointly estimates the model parameters, providing a procedure for fitting the coupled mixtures. Experiments in document analysis and image modeling demonstrate the construction in two application areas, illustrating how the same sharing framework can support different kinds of data.
neurips-2012-coupling-nonparametric-mixt.tldr: Latent Dirichlet processes let related mixture models share components through flexible many-to-many relationships.

paragraphs: The paper presents a faster way to compute weighted V-statistics in resampling problems involving either univariate or multivariate data. Directly working through resampled arrangements can create an enormous computational burden. The authors replace explicit resampling with an algebraic formulation designed to exploit relationships among the arrangements that would otherwise be processed.

The key step connects resampling to a finite group action and reformulates the calculation as orbit enumeration. Orbits organize arrangements according to the symmetries induced by that action. This gives the algorithm a structured way to account for related cases without carrying out the corresponding resampling operations individually.

To reduce the work further, the method lists orbits by symmetry order and recursively computes sums for both index functions and data functions. The complexity analysis reports a reduction from factorial or n-to-the-n cost to a low-order polynomial. The significance is computational: recognizing symmetry changes how the required statistical calculation is organized and makes a much larger reduction possible.
neurips-2012-fast-resampling-weighted-v-.tldr: A symmetry-based reformulation computes weighted V-statistics without explicit resampling, reducing the analyzed cost to low-order polynomial complexity.

paragraphs: The paper considers regression problems in which the target function changes more strongly along some input coordinates than others. For methods that predict using distances between examples, this uneven sensitivity matters: the coordinate system used to compare inputs should reflect how the output varies. The paper develops a way to estimate and use that information.

Its proposal assigns each coordinate a weight based on an estimated norm of the target function’s derivative in that direction. The derivative norm summarizes the function’s sensitivity to that coordinate. These weights are then used by distance-based regression methods, including kernel regression and nearest-neighbor regression, to improve how input differences are assessed.

The authors give a simple estimator for the derivative norms and prove that it is consistent. They also show that it can be learned efficiently online. Their stated finding is that this weighting can significantly improve regression performance, connecting the choice of input distance to estimated properties of the function being learned.
neurips-2012-gradient-weights-help-nonpa.tldr: Estimating how strongly a target function varies along each coordinate provides effective distance weights for kernel and nearest-neighbor regression.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to locate multiple changes in a sequence when the number of changes is unknown. Its focus is time-series data with potentially strong dependence between observations. In this setting, treating successive measurements as independent would exclude the kinds of sequences the authors want to handle.

The authors propose a consistency framework and an algorithm that is asymptotically consistent within it. The stated distributional assumption is stationary ergodicity: the generating time-series distributions have stable statistical behavior and support long-run regularity. They impose no independence or parametric assumptions, and permit dependence to take an arbitrary form.

This matters because the guarantee is formulated around broad properties of the generating processes rather than a particular model of their dependence. The asymptotic qualification places the result in the limit of increasing data, rather than promising exact answers for every finite sequence. Experimental evaluations complement the theory, supplying an empirical examination of an approach designed for highly dependent observations.
neurips-2012-locating-changes-in-highly-.tldr: The paper proposes asymptotically consistent change-point estimation for stationary ergodic time series with arbitrary dependence and an unknown number of changes.

paragraphs: The paper addresses instability in approximate probabilistic inference based on the Bethe free energy. Existing message-passing procedures seek stationary points, but their updates do not distinguish minima from maxima and may fail to converge. In continuous problems, this instability is connected to invalid intermediate probability estimates, including Gaussian distributions assigned negative variances.

The proposed approach treats inference as constrained minimization. It uses multiplier methods with established convergence properties and bound projections that keep marginal approximations within valid distribution families at every iteration. Validity therefore becomes an explicit part of the optimization process, addressing a concrete failure mode of the message-passing dynamics.

The authors derive algorithms for discrete and Gaussian pairwise Markov random fields and report improvements over standard loopy belief propagation. They also evaluate a model combining discrete and continuous variables, reporting improvements over expectation propagation. The contribution brings convergent optimization and valid intermediate estimates together; its stated convergence result does not imply that every solution is a global minimum.
neurips-2012-minimization-of-continuous-.tldr: Constrained Bethe minimization keeps intermediate probability estimates valid and provides convergent alternatives to unstable message-passing updates.

paragraphs: The paper studies how related prediction tasks can learn a sparse set of shared features. Sharing useful features is intended to improve generalization across tasks. Many existing approaches use convex sparse regularization, but the authors identify a weakness: these penalties can be loose approximations to the desired penalty on how many features are used.

They introduce a nonconvex regularizer and an associated formulation for multitask feature learning. To solve the resulting optimization problem, they propose the Multi-Stage Multi-Task Feature Learning algorithm, or MSMTFL. The multi-stage procedure is the computational counterpart of changing the regularizer, making the proposed formulation usable as a learning method.

The theoretical analysis establishes a better parameter-estimation error bound than the convex formulation. This is a statement about the derived bound, rather than a guarantee of superiority on every dataset. Experiments on synthetic and real data also demonstrate effectiveness against state-of-the-art multitask sparse feature-learning methods, supporting the practical value of the proposed formulation and algorithm.
neurips-2012-multi-stage-multi-task-feat.tldr: MSMTFL uses a nonconvex shared-feature penalty and multi-stage optimization to improve parameter-estimation bounds over a convex formulation.

paragraphs: The paper develops a multiclass learning framework built around simplex coding, a coordinated way to encode class labels and decode predictions. The motivation is to extend a relaxation approach commonly used for binary classification to problems with several classes. The coding strategy supplies the structure needed to carry that approach into the multiclass setting.

Within this framework, the authors analyze relaxation error without imposing constraints on the hypothesis class under consideration. That matters because the analysis can address the relationship between the relaxed learning problem and classification without depending on such restrictions. The encoding and decoding are therefore part of the theoretical foundation, as well as the prediction procedure.

The authors also derive regularized methods with provable consistency and training and tuning complexity independent of the number of classes. They describe these as the first methods with that combination of properties. Convex-analysis tools developed for the framework are additionally presented as applicable beyond the specific multiclass construction studied here.
neurips-2012-multiclass-learning-with-si.tldr: Simplex coding supports consistent regularized multiclass learning methods whose stated training and tuning complexity is independent of class count.

paragraphs: The paper introduces iKBSF for learning sequential decisions from incoming data in a continuous state space. It extends kernel-based reinforcement learning to an online setting. A central concern is memory: processing more experience becomes difficult when the representation must keep growing with the number of observed transitions.

iKBSF has space complexity independent of the number of sample transitions, allowing it to process an arbitrary amount of data without sample-count-driven memory growth. The authors also describe stability and favorable convergence properties. Their theoretical result shows that it can approximate, to any desired accuracy, the value function learned by an equivalent batch kernel-based approximator.

That comparison links the incremental procedure to the output of a corresponding batch method; it is not a claim of arbitrary accuracy relative to the optimal policy itself. The authors apply iKBSF to three-pole balancing, where processing many transitions is crucial for high success rates. This application illustrates why bounded dependence on accumulated data matters operationally.
neurips-2012-on-line-reinforcement-learn.tldr: iKBSF processes online reinforcement-learning experience with memory independent of sample count while approximating an equivalent batch kernel method.

paragraphs: The paper develops stochastic optimization methods for regularized objectives in which both the loss and regularizer may be nonsmooth. Its starting point is regularized dual averaging. The goal is to achieve optimal convergence rates across both convex and strongly convex losses while preserving useful properties of the regularized solution.

For strongly convex losses, the proposed algorithm achieves O(1/N + 1/N²) after N iterations, improving on the previous O(log N/N) rate cited for stochastic dual averaging. It also constructs the final solution directly through a proximal mapping instead of averaging all past iterates. With sparsity-inducing penalties such as the l1 norm, this construction encourages sparser solutions.

The authors further build a multi-stage method that uses the new algorithm as a subroutine. For strongly convex losses, this extension achieves the stated uniformly optimal rate O(1/N + exp(-N)). The results connect faster convergence guarantees with an output construction suited to sparse regularization, addressing both optimization efficiency and the form of the learned solution.
neurips-2012-optimal-regularized-dual-av.tldr: New regularized dual averaging methods attain optimal stochastic convergence rates and construct outputs in a way that encourages sparsity.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why variational Bayesian estimation can work well in probabilistic principal component analysis. One motivating puzzle is that variational approximations sometimes produce sparse solutions even when that behavior is rarely seen in full Bayesian estimation. The authors seek a theoretical explanation for a useful aspect of the approximation.

They focus on the case where noise variance is unknown and derive a sufficient condition for recovering the true PCA dimensionality perfectly. The result applies in a large-scale limit as the observed matrix grows without bound. Both qualifications matter: the condition guarantees recovery in the analyzed limit, and is not presented as a necessary condition.

The analysis also yields bounds for a noise-variance estimator and simple closed-form solutions for other parameters. These are useful computational outputs as well as parts of the theory, with the authors identifying their value for implementing variational Bayesian PCA. The paper thus links dimensionality selection to both an asymptotic guarantee and more explicit parameter calculations.
neurips-2012-perfect-dimensionality-reco.tldr: The paper gives a sufficient asymptotic condition for variational Bayesian PCA to recover the true dimensionality when noise variance is unknown.

paragraphs: The paper develops density estimation for distributions whose possible values lie within a bounded region. It also allows hard constraints on that region’s topology. The aim is to learn a probability model that respects structural restrictions on where data can occur, making those restrictions part of the model itself.

The approach combines kernel-based learning with persistent homology and other tools from computational algebraic topology. These tools allow algebraic-topological information to be encoded as constraints during density estimation. The authors emphasize that this addresses structural requirements not handled by the probabilistic models they compare with conceptually.

They examine the method on two synthetic examples at several sample sizes and apply it to learning a racecar motion model from real data. In that application, the learned model respects the racetrack’s underlying topology and consequently constrains the car’s trajectories. This example explains the practical role of the constraints: a density model can incorporate the structure that governs which movements are possible.
neurips-2012-persistent-homology-for-lea.tldr: Combining persistent homology with kernel methods enables bounded-support density models that obey hard topological constraints.

paragraphs: The study asks whether intracranial brain signals can predict which hand a person will raise before a movement cue appears. Epilepsy patients with electrodes implanted for clinical purposes played a matching-pennies game. After a five-second countdown, they raised either hand at the go signal, winning or losing money depending on their opponent’s choice.

Combined low-frequency local field potentials from ten electrodes carried information about the upcoming hand choice. In two patients, an online system predicted the hand half a second before the go signal with 68±3% accuracy. This establishes the reported real-time result in the specific task and patient setting studied.

The authors then built a system tracking up to thirty electrodes and evaluated it retrospectively on data from seven patients. Average accuracy was 83%, rising to 92% when the system withheld predictions on the least confident 30% of trials. These retrospective results distinguish broader signal use and selective prediction from the earlier online demonstration, while supporting the feasibility of predicting individual binary actions before they occur.
neurips-2012-predicting-action-content-o.tldr: Intracranial signals predicted upcoming hand choices before the cue in two patients online, with higher accuracies reported in separate retrospective evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn calibrated class probabilities when training labels are ambiguous. Each example comes with several candidate categories, at most one of which is true. The goal is to obtain meaningful posterior probabilities despite this incomplete supervision, rather than treating the observed candidate set as a fully resolved class label.

The authors generalize proper losses to this setting. A proper loss aligns the learning objective with estimating the relevant probabilities. They establish a necessary and sufficient condition for propriety and give a direct construction that converts a conventional proper loss into one suitable for partial labels.

The analysis represents the relationship between true classes and observed labels through a mixing probability matrix. A notable result is that constructing useful proper losses does not require knowing that entire matrix. The authors also show that losses can be proper on a subset of the probability simplex. This qualification identifies a restricted region of class-probability distributions where the desired property holds.
neurips-2012-proper-losses-for-learning-.tldr: The paper characterizes and constructs proper probability-estimation losses for ambiguous labels, including constructions that do not need the full label-mixing matrix.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a tension between conventional utility-based decision theory and observed human choices. In the conventional account described by the authors, options have their own scalar utilities. Yet people can change their preferences systematically when the available choice set changes, challenging an explanation based on fixed option-specific desirability.

The proposed theory treats desirability as something inferred through comparisons among the options available at a particular decision. Values can therefore depend on the current choice context. The authors show that this relative approach provides a rational account of behaviors previously regarded as difficult violations of rational choice.

They also characterize conditions under which an agent choosing the best option through dynamic value inference behaves exactly like an agent governed by a static ordinal utility function. This connects the new account to familiar preference rankings. Context-sensitive inference can explain departures from fixed preferences, while under the identified conditions it produces the same observable choices as a stable ordering.
neurips-2012-rational-inference-of-relat.tldr: A theory of relative value inference explains context-dependent preferences and identifies when they coincide with a static utility ranking.

paragraphs: The paper introduces RO-TD, a temporal-difference learning method that combines off-policy convergence with sparse value-function representations. Off-policy learning uses experience to evaluate a policy that may differ from the one producing that experience. The method adds l1 regularization to select useful features while keeping computational costs low.

Its framework joins two ideas: convergent gradient temporal-difference methods, such as TDC, and a convex-concave saddle-point formulation for nonsmooth convex optimization. This formulation permits first-order solvers and online convex regularization. The combination makes feature selection part of the value-learning process while retaining the off-policy convergence focus of the underlying gradient methods.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental analyses of the resulting algorithm. Their experiments illustrate convergence in off-policy learning, sparse feature selection, and low computational cost. These findings address three connected demands on a value estimator: learning stably from the available experience, representing values with fewer active features, and making those updates computationally manageable.
neurips-2012-regularized-off-policy-td-l.tldr: RO-TD combines convergent off-policy temporal-difference learning with online l1 regularization to learn sparse value representations at low computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the drop in performance that occurs when an object detector trained on still images is applied to video. Its setup provides labeled images but only unlabeled target videos. The task is therefore to adapt across domains without requiring manually labeled examples from the video domain.

The proposed self-paced procedure repeatedly retrains the detector using automatically discovered video examples, beginning with the easiest ones. As adaptation progresses, it increases the number of target examples and reduces the number from the image source. To find useful examples in large video collections, it scores trajectory tracks rather than individual bounding boxes.

The framework can also incorporate expressive features specific to video, giving adaptation access to information suited to the target domain. Evaluations on the 2011 TRECVID Multimedia Event Detection and LabelMe Video datasets produce promising results. The stated benefit is supported by those experiments: progressively shifting training toward selected video examples can help transfer image detectors to video.
neurips-2012-shifting-weights-adapting-o.tldr: Self-paced domain adaptation improves image-to-video detector transfer by progressively training on automatically selected video tracks.

paragraphs: The paper considers supervised learning when data are accessible only through pairwise similarity scores, including similarities that are not positive semidefinite. Previous work had concentrated on classification. The authors propose a broader model intended to cover general supervised tasks while including the earlier classification framework.

They define what makes a similarity function good for a particular task and adapt a landmarking technique to obtain efficient algorithms from such functions. For real-valued regression, ordinal regression, and ranking, they establish bounded generalization error. In real-valued regression, an additional goodness definition combined with a sparse-recovery result yields a sparse predictor with a generalization bound.

Experiments examine regression and ordinal regression with non-positive-semidefinite similarities. The authors report particularly strong results for sparse landmark selection, which improves accuracy over their baselines while reducing computational cost. The contribution connects task-specific conditions on similarity quality to both learning guarantees and practical algorithms, extending the usefulness of similarity-based access beyond classification.
neurips-2012-supervised-learning-with-si.tldr: Task-specific similarity conditions and landmarking support efficient regression and ranking with generalization guarantees, including sparse predictors.
